name: 1986 price collapse
explanation: The IMF reports that Saudi Arabia's production had dropped to 2.3 million b/d by 1985, after which it raised production, abandoned official pricing and adopted a spot pricing mechanism. The IMF cites weak demand and rising non-OPEC output as the background.
source_1_publisher: IMF Finance & Development, Down the Slide (Dec 2015)
notes: Source check Oct 7: the EIA PDF is a scanned image and could not be read by machine; read it by eye before adding EIA's monthly figures (netback pricing, 4.5 million b/d in January 1986).

name: 1990 invasion of Kuwait and the January 1991 fall
explanation: EIA reports peak lost production of about 4.3 million b/d of combined Iraqi and Kuwaiti crude. On January 16, 1991 the US announced air strikes and a release from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; the Department of Energy says the release helped calm the global oil market and prices began to moderate.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Effects of crude oil supply disruptions
source_2_publisher: US Department of Energy, History of SPR releases
notes: Source check Oct 7: the $16 and $28 price figures were removed (from EIA's Energy Kids timeline, not the cited article).

name: 1997 to 1998 lows
explanation: EIA's April 1998 outlook named increased worldwide production, low winter fuel demand and the Asian financial crisis as contributors to falling prices, and noted that Iraq was increasing production. EIA notes WTI fell to almost $10 per barrel in late 1998.
source_2_publisher: EIA STEO supplement, Why are oil prices so high?
notes: Source check Oct 7: the OPEC 10% quota increase was removed (not in the cited sources).

name: The run to the 2008 peak and the 2008 to 2009 crash
explanation: The Federal Reserve's 2008 annual report links the rise of WTI above $145 by mid-July 2008 to robust demand, especially from emerging economies, and restrained near-term supply, and the fall that followed to financial market turmoil and the downturn in global activity, with WTI down about 75% from its peak by January 2009.
source_2_publisher: EIA working paper, Factors influencing oil prices
notes: Researchers disagree about the role of speculation in 2008; the working paper surveys the views.

name: 2011: Libya and the Brent minus WTI blowout
explanation: EIA reports Brent rose $15 between February 18 and March 2, 2011 as the market coped with the loss of 1.5 million b/d of Libyan exports, while rising inland supply and transport bottlenecks near Cushing held WTI at a discount. EIA puts the record Brent premium at $29.70 on September 22, 2011.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Brent averages over $100 in 2011
source_2_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, WTI-Brent spread narrows
notes: Source check Oct 7: in this project's daily spot data the spread was $28.92 on Sep 22, 2011 and peaked at $29.59 on Sep 23; EIA's $29.70 is likely a different price basis.

name: The 2014 to 2016 collapse
explanation: EIA reports Brent and WTI fell from monthly averages of $112 and $105 in June 2014 to $62 and $59 in December, as robust global production exceeded demand, and US crude output rose 1.2 million b/d in 2014. EIA reports a sustained excess of supply over demand in 2015, and prices ended 2015 below $40.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Crude oil prices down sharply in fourth quarter of 2014
source_2_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Crude oil prices ended 2015 lower
notes: Source check Oct 7: removed '50%', 'weakening demand', 'fewer supply disruptions' (EIA reports disruptions rose in 2014) and the OPEC 30 million b/d target (not in the cited articles).

name: September 2019 Abqaiq attack
explanation: EIA reports an attack on September 14, 2019 damaged the Abqaiq processing facility and the Khurais field. On September 16, the first full trading day after, Brent and WTI had their largest one-day increase in a decade, and both fell on September 17 after Saudi Aramco said output would be restored by the end of the month.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Saudi Arabia crude oil production outage
notes: The article does not state the barrels taken offline (see news reader demo).

name: April 2020: WTI below zero
explanation: The CFTC reports the May 2020 WTI futures contract settled at -$37.63 on April 20, the day before it expired. EIA reports Cushing storage was 76% full as of April 17 and consumption had sharply declined. A CFTC staff report described several coinciding factors without assigning a root cause.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Low liquidity and limited storage pushed WTI futures below zero
source_2_publisher: CFTC staff interim report on WTI trading around April 20, 2020
notes: Source check Oct 7: -$37.63 is from the CFTC, not EIA. EIA's daily spot WTI series (this database) shows -$36.98 that day; futures settlement and spot are different prices.

name: 2022 Russia invasion spike
explanation: EIA reports the front-month Brent futures contract settled above $100 on February 28, 2022, after Russia's further invasion of Ukraine. EIA reports that on March 8 the invasion combined with low global inventories lifted the price to its highest inflation-adjusted level since 2014.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Crude oil prices in 2022
source_2_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Crude oil prices rise above $100
notes: Source check Oct 7: Feb 28 is a futures settlement; this database's EIA spot Brent first passed $100 on Feb 14, 2022 and was $133.18 on Mar 8. The $134 figure was removed (not in the cited articles).

name: Red Sea shipping attacks from late 2023 (a disruption without a price spike)
explanation: EIA reports attacks on commercial ships in the Red Sea began in November 2023; crude flows through Bab el-Mandeb were 18% lower in December than in January to November, and some vessels went around southern Africa. EIA reports Brent traded in a range, from $82 in the week before the attacks to $79 on January 18, 2024.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Red Sea attacks increase shipping times and freight rates
notes: Compare with Cape of Good Hope and Bab el-Mandeb transits in chokepoint_transit. The database shows Bab el-Mandeb tanker transits at 114% of the 2019 to 2025 median over Nov 2023 to Feb 2024; that median includes the low rerouting years 2024 and 2025, and ship counts are not barrels, so it does not contradict EIA's 18% lower crude flow.

name: June 2025 Israel and Iran fighting
explanation: EIA reports Brent (futures, per the article's link) rose from $69 on June 12 to $74 on June 13, 2025, and that maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was not blocked as of June 16.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Strait of Hormuz remains critical oil chokepoint
notes: A risk event: no barrels lost per the source. This database's EIA spot Brent was $70.84 and $76.00 on those days.

name: The 2026 Strait of Hormuz disruption
explanation: EIA reports Brent front-month futures rose from $61 at the start of 2026 to $118 at the end of the first quarter, surpassing $100 on March 12, as Iraq, Saudi Arabia and the UAE shut in oil production; EIA says the quarter's increase was the largest on an inflation-adjusted basis in data going back to 1988. The episode's sub-events are rows W01 to W14 of data/iran_war_2026.csv.
source_1_publisher: EIA Today in Energy, Prices increased sharply in the first quarter of 2026
source_2_publisher: IEA commentary on the Strait of Hormuz shock (not reachable at iea.org on Oct 7)
notes: Source check Oct 7: '7.5 million b/d shut in during March' is not in EIA article 67424 and was removed. The IEA figure (flows from about 20 to an average of 2.7 million b/d in March to May) was seen only in a reprint credited to the IEA, dated June 29, 2026; confirm at iea.org before use. $61 and $118 are futures; EIA spot Brent was $126.69 on March 31.
